examFormat.mix: Conceptual questions, including definitions and 'Which is NOT...' multiple choice.
examFormat.notes: Based on classmate intel, the exam focuses heavily on definitions and distinguishing between concepts.

verifiedPatterns.pattern: ★ Define key terminology from databases, BI, and project management (e.g., Cardinality, ETL, Critical Path, Taxonomy).
★ Answer 'Which of the following is NOT...' questions for topics like Project Management responsibilities, LMS functions, and the ETL process.
★ Distinguish between related concepts, such as Digital vs. Analog, Data Warehouse vs. Data Mart, and Client/Server models.
★ Know the hierarchy of data storage units, from Bytes to Terabytes and beyond.

topics.name: Database Fundamentals
topics.why: Exam tests core database concepts like cardinality, relationships, keys, and normalization. These are foundational for understanding how data is structured and managed.

topics.name: Business Intelligence & Analytics
topics.why: Questions cover the BI infrastructure, including ETL processes, data warehouses, and analytics types. Know what ETL is and what it is NOT.

topics.name: Project Management
topics.why: Confirmed questions on critical path, risk management, and the responsibilities of project management. Understand the triple constraint (Scope, Time, Resources).

topics.name: Hardware, Networking & Cloud
topics.why: Exam requires knowing data storage units (Bytes, GB, TB), digital vs. analog signals, and client-server models like 'thin client'.

topics.name: Knowledge Management & Data Concepts
topics.why: A significant number of verified exam terms fall under this topic: knowledge management, taxonomy, crowdsourcing, conversion rate, and communities of practice.

topics.name: Data Visualization
topics.why: Principles of data visualization are a confirmed topic. This includes understanding the purpose of different chart types and dashboarding concepts from Tableau.

formulas.name: Basic SQL Query Structure
formulas.vars: [columns] fields to show · [table] source table · [condition] filter criteria (e.g., PART.Supplier_Number = SUPPLIER.Supplier_Number)
formulas.when: Querying a relational database.
formulas.trap: Forgetting to join tables in the WHERE clause for multi-table queries will produce a Cartesian product (all possible row combinations), which is WRONG.
formulas.ex: SELECT Part_Name, Supplier_Name FROM PART, SUPPLIER WHERE PART.Supplier_Number = SUPPLIER.Supplier_Number; ✓

formulas.name: Project Triple Constraint
formulas.vars: Scope: what the project will deliver (quality, risk) · Time: deadline · Resources: budget, people, tools
formulas.when: Managing any project.
formulas.trap: Thinking you can change one constraint (e.g., increase scope) without impacting at least one other is FALSE. You MUST adjust time or resources.
formulas.ex: Client wants a new feature (↑ Scope). You must increase the budget (↑ Resources) or extend the deadline (↑ Time). ✓

formulas.name: Slack Time Calculation
formulas.formula: Slack Time = Late Start - Early Start
formulas.vars: Late Start: latest a task can start without delaying project · Early Start: earliest a task can begin
formulas.when: Analyzing a project schedule to find non-critical tasks.
formulas.trap: Tasks on the critical path have zero slack. Any delay in these tasks is WRONG to ignore as it directly delays the entire project.

formulas.name: Data Storage Conversion
formulas.formula:
1 Terabyte (TB) = 1,024 Gigabytes (GB)
1 Gigabyte (GB) = 1,024 Megabytes (MB)
1 Megabyte (MB) = 1,024 Kilobytes (KB)
1 Kilobyte (KB) = 1,024 Bytes
formulas.vars: Each unit is 2^10 (1,024) times larger than the previous one.
formulas.when: Comparing file sizes or storage capacities.
formulas.trap: Using 1,000 instead of 1,024 for conversions is incorrect in most OS contexts (base-2), though storage manufacturers sometimes use base-10 (1,000). For this class, use 1,024.
formulas.ex: A 2TB drive has 2 * 1,024 = 2,048 GB of space. ✓

formulas.name: SQL SELECT with JOIN
formulas.formula: SELECT T1.col, T2.col FROM Table1 T1 JOIN Table2 T2 ON T1.key = T2.key WHERE condition;
formulas.vars: T1, T2 table aliases · col column name · key joining field
formulas.when: Retrieving data from two or more related tables.
formulas.ex: SELECT PART.Part_Name, SUPPLIER.Supplier_Name FROM PART JOIN SUPPLIER ON PART.Supplier_Number = SUPPLIER.Supplier_Number WHERE PART.Unit_Price > 20.00;

formulas.name: SQL SELECT with OR
formulas.formula: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE condition1 OR condition2;
formulas.vars: condition1, condition2 boolean expressions
formulas.when: Selecting rows that satisfy at least one of multiple conditions.
formulas.ex: To get parts 137 and 150: ... WHERE Part_Number = 137 OR Part_Number = 150; ✓

formulas.name: SQL SELECT with AND
formulas.formula: SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE condition1 AND condition2;
formulas.vars: condition1, condition2 boolean expressions
formulas.when: Selecting rows that must satisfy all specified conditions.
formulas.ex: To get part 137 from its supplier: ... WHERE PART.Supplier_Number = SUPPLIER.Supplier_Number AND Part_Number = 137; ✓

formulas.name: Earned Value (EV)
formulas.vars: % Complete actual percentage of work completed · BAC Budget at Completion (total planned budget)
formulas.when: Measuring project performance against the financial plan.
formulas.ex: Project budget (BAC) is $100k. 25% of the work is done. EV = 0.25 × $100,000 = $25,000. ✓

formulas.name: Cost Variance (CV)
formulas.vars: EV Earned Value · AC Actual Cost
formulas.when: Determining if the project is over or under budget. Negative is bad.
formulas.ex: EV is $25k, but actual cost (AC) is $30k. CV = $25k - $30k = -$5k. Project is $5k over budget. ⚠

formulas.name: Schedule Variance (SV)
formulas.vars: EV Earned Value · PV Planned Value (budgeted cost of work scheduled)
formulas.when: Determining if the project is ahead or behind schedule. Negative is bad.
formulas.ex: EV is $25k. We planned to have $35k of work done by now (PV). SV = $25k - $35k = -$10k. Project is behind schedule. ⚠

formulas.name: Tableau Calculated Field
formulas.vars: [Profit] a field in the data source
formulas.when: Creating a new dimension or measure based on existing data in Tableau.
formulas.ex: Creates a new dimension that categorizes each record based on its profit value.

formulas.name: URL Structure
formulas.vars: protocol e.g., http · hostname e.g., www.megacorp.com · path e.g., /content/features/
formulas.when: Identifying the components of a web address.

formulas.name: SQL SELECT with OR Condition
formulas.formula: SELECT col1, col2 FROM table1, table2 WHERE table1.key = table2.key AND (condition1 OR condition2);
formulas.vars: col column name · table table name · key matching primary/foreign key columns
formulas.when: Selecting rows that meet at least one of several conditions, after joining tables.
formulas.ex: SELECT Part_Number, Part_Name, Supplier_Name FROM PART, SUPPLIER WHERE PART.Supplier_Number = SUPPLIER.Supplier_Number AND (Part_Number = 137 OR Part_Number = 150); → Returns parts 137 and 150 with their supplier names. ✓

formulas.name: SQL SELECT with ORDER BY
formulas.formula: SELECT column_list FROM table_name WHERE condition ORDER BY column_name [ASC|DESC];
formulas.vars: ASC ascending order (default) · DESC descending order
formulas.when: You need to sort the results of a query.
formulas.trap: Forgetting to specify DESC is a common error; results will default to ASC (ascending) order.
formulas.ex: SELECT Part_Name, Unit_Price FROM PART ORDER BY Unit_Price DESC; → Lists all parts, starting with the most expensive (Compressor, 54.00). ✓

formulas.name: Excel VLOOKUP for Relational Data
formulas.vars: lookup_value what to look for · table_array where to look · col_index_num which column to return · range_lookup EXACT (FALSE) or APPROXIMATE (TRUE) match
formulas.when: Simulating a relational database join in Excel to pull data from one table into another based on a common key.
formulas.ex: In a sales sheet, to find a student's name from their ID (1325): =VLOOKUP(1325, StudentTable, 2, FALSE) → Returns 'BAKER, ANDREA'. ✓

formulas.name: Data Storage Conversion (GB to Bytes)
formulas.vars: GB Gigabyte · MB Megabyte · KB Kilobyte
formulas.when: Converting between storage capacity units. Each step up is a factor of 1,024.
formulas.trap: Using 1,000 instead of 1,024 for conversions is WRONG for binary storage measurement.

formulas.name: SQL SELECT Specific Columns
formulas.vars: column1, column2 specific fields to display
formulas.when: You need to view only certain fields from a table, not all of them.
formulas.ex: SELECT Supplier_Name, Supplier_City FROM SUPPLIER; → Shows only the names and cities of all suppliers, hiding street, state, etc. ✓

formulas.name: SQL SELECT All Columns
formulas.vars: * a wildcard representing all columns
formulas.when: You need to view all fields from a table.
formulas.ex: SELECT * FROM PART; → Shows Part_Number, Part_Name, Unit_Price, and Supplier_Number for all parts in the table. ✓

formulas.name: URL Component Breakdown
formulas.vars: protocol e.g., http · hostname e.g., www.megacorp.com · path e.g., /content/features/ · filename e.g., 082602.html
formulas.when: Deconstructing a web address to understand its parts.

formulas.name: Project Slack Time
formulas.formula: Slack Time = Late Start Time - Early Start Time
formulas.vars: Late Start latest a task can start without delaying project · Early Start earliest a task can begin
formulas.when: Determining how much a task can be delayed without affecting the project's final deadline. Critical path tasks have zero slack.
formulas.ex: If a task's Early Start is Day 3 and its Late Start is Day 5, Slack Time = 5 - 3 = 2 days. The task can be delayed up to 2 days. ✓

concepts.def: Describes the relationship between two tables in a database in terms of the number of rows in one table that can be related to rows in another. The lines connecting tables in a diagram show cardinality. Common types are one-to-one, one-to-many, and many-to-many. Example: One student can have many course enrollments (one-to-many).

The sequence of tasks in a project which, if delayed, will delay the entire project's completion. It is the longest path through the project network, and tasks on this path have zero slack. Example: If 'Build Foundation' and 'Frame House' are on the critical path, a 2-day delay in pouring the foundation will delay the project finish date by 2 days.

A three-phase process where data is extracted from various source systems, transformed (cleansed, standardized, normalized), and then loaded into a target data warehouse. Example: Extracting daily sales data from multiple stores, transforming date formats to be consistent (MM/DD/YYYY), and loading the cleaned data into the central sales data warehouse.

A computer that runs from resources stored on a central server instead of a localized hard drive. It works by connecting to a server-based environment which hosts most of the applications, memory, and sensitive data. The exam answer is 'thin client'. Example: A call center computer that boots up and loads its operating system and applications directly from the company's main server.

Malicious software or hardware that records the keystrokes made by a user on a computer. Its purpose is to steal sensitive information like passwords, credit card numbers, and personal messages. A hardware version can be a small USB device called a 'rubber ducky'. Example: An attacker installs a keylogger on a public computer to capture the login credentials of everyone who uses it.

Digital signals use discrete, binary values (0s and 1s) to represent information. Analog signals use continuous physical waves. Digital is more resistant to noise and can be perfectly copied. Example: A modern computer processes data digitally (binary code), while an old vinyl record stores music as analog grooves in the plastic.

The process of creating, sharing, using, and managing the knowledge and information of an organization. It refers to a multidisciplinary approach to achieving organizational objectives by making the best use of knowledge. Example: A company creating a central wiki (like Confluence) where engineers document solutions to common problems for others to reference.

The process of identifying, assessing, and controlling threats to an organization's capital and earnings. In project management, this involves determining potential risks and developing strategies to mitigate them. Example: A project manager identifies 'key developer might quit' as a risk and mitigates it by ensuring code is well-documented and another developer is cross-trained.

The practice and science of classification of things or concepts, including the principles that underlie such classification. In IT, it refers to the hierarchical organization of information. Example: A website's navigation menu is a taxonomy, organizing products into categories like 'Electronics' -> 'Laptops' -> 'Gaming Laptops'.

In web analytics, the percentage of users who take a desired action. The 'conversion' is the act of a visitor completing a site goal. Example: If an e-commerce site has 100 visitors and 5 of them make a purchase, the conversion rate is 5%.

The practice of obtaining information or input into a task or project by enlisting the services of a large number of people, either paid or unpaid, typically via the Internet. Example: The website Waze uses crowdsourcing by collecting real-time traffic data from its users' phones to provide the best driving routes.

A group of people who share a concern or a passion for something they do and learn how to do it better as they interact regularly. It's a key concept in knowledge management. Example: A group of software developers at a company who specialize in Python and meet weekly to share new techniques and solve common problems.

An architectural model where the majority of processing and logic is performed on the server, not the client machine. This is characteristic of systems using thin clients. The exam answer is 'server concentric'. Example: A web-based application like Google Docs, where all the document processing happens on Google's servers and the user's browser just displays the result.

A software application for the administration, documentation, tracking, reporting, and delivery of educational courses or training programs. Example: Blackboard or Canvas, which universities use to host course materials, assignments, and grades.

A Data Warehouse stores current and historical data from many core systems across the entire enterprise. A Data Mart is a smaller, focused subset of a data warehouse that deals with a single subject or line of business. Example: A company's main data warehouse contains all sales, HR, and supply chain data. The marketing department uses a data mart that contains only customer and sales data for their specific analyses.

The process of organizing columns and tables in a relational database to minimize data redundancy. It involves dividing larger tables into smaller, well-structured tables and defining relationships between them. Example: Instead of storing 'DeptName' in every employee record (redundant), create a separate 'Department' table and link to it with a 'DeptNo' foreign key.

A Primary Key is a field that uniquely identifies each record in a table. A Foreign Key is a primary key from one table that is used in a second table to form a link between them. Example: In a 'Students' table, 'StudentID' is the primary key. In a 'Course_Enrollments' table, 'StudentID' is a foreign key linking back to the 'Students' table.

Descriptive: What happened? (e.g., financial reports). Predictive: What will happen? (e.g., sales projections). Prescriptive: What should we do? (e.g., optimization models). Organizations mature from descriptive to prescriptive analytics.

A tool for multidimensional data analysis, allowing users to quickly analyze information that has been summarized into multidimensional views (cubes). It enables slicing, dicing, and drilling down into data. Example: Using a pivot table in Excel to analyze sales data by region, product, and time period.

Cloud service models. IaaS (Infrastructure): Vendor manages hardware (servers, storage). You manage OS, apps. PaaS (Platform): Vendor manages hardware + OS/middleware. You manage apps, data. SaaS (Software): Vendor manages everything. You just use the app. Example: AWS EC2 (IaaS), Heroku (PaaS), Gmail (SaaS).

A method of slicing digital messages into small parcels (packets), sending them along different communication paths as available, and reassembling them at the destination. It is the primary basis for data communication in computer networks like the Internet. Example: When you load a webpage, its components (text, images) are broken into packets, sent over the internet, and reassembled by your browser.

A secure, encrypted connection over a public network (like the Internet) to a private network. It encrypts messages to protect them from snooping. Example: Connecting to your company's VPN from home to securely access internal files and servers as if you were in the office.

Dimensions are qualitative, categorical values that set the level of detail (e.g., Region, Product Category). Measures are quantitative, numerical values that can be aggregated (e.g., Sales, Profit). In Tableau, Dimensions are typically blue, and Measures are green. Example: Analyzing 'Sales' (Measure) by 'Region' (Dimension).

Joins combine tables by adding more columns of data on a row-by-row basis from the same data source. Blends combine data from multiple, separate data sources at an aggregate level by linking on common dimension fields. Example: Joining 'Orders' and 'Returns' tables from one Excel file. Blending aggregated sales data from a SQL database with sales goal data from a separate Excel file.

A type of bar chart that illustrates a project schedule. It lists tasks on the vertical axis and time intervals on the horizontal axis. The width of the horizontal bars shows the duration of each task. Example: A Gantt chart for building a house would show tasks like 'Lay Foundation' and 'Framing' with bars indicating their start dates, end dates, and dependencies.

A Sheet is a single data visualization (e.g., one bar chart). A Dashboard is a collection of multiple sheets and other objects arranged on a single screen. A Story is a sequence of visualizations or dashboards that work together to convey a narrative.

concepts.def: Data are raw, unorganized facts. Information is data that has been processed, organized, and structured into a meaningful context. Example: A list of sale amounts is data; a report showing sales trends by region is information.

A set of rules a database uses to ensure relationships between tables remain consistent. It prevents creating records that reference non-existent records. Example: Prevents adding an order for a `CustomerID` that does not exist in the `Customers` table.

A project that is significantly over budget, behind schedule, and/or fails to deliver the specified performance. Statistics suggest 30-40% of IT projects fall into this category. Example: A new CRM system planned for 6 months and $1M ends up taking 18 months and costing $3M.

A hierarchical decomposition of the total scope of work to be carried out by a project team. It breaks down the project into smaller, more manageable components. Example: For a 'Build Website' project, top-level WBS items might be 'Design', 'Development', and 'Testing', each with sub-tasks.

The foundational suite of communication protocols for the internet. TCP handles breaking data into packets and reassembling them, while IP handles addressing and routing the packets to their destination. Example: When you load a webpage, TCP/IP manages the entire data transfer process.

An open-source framework for distributed parallel processing of massive datasets (Big Data) across clusters of inexpensive computers. Example: A social media company uses Hadoop to process terabytes of daily user activity logs to identify trends.
Specialized software stored in non-volatile, read-only memory on a hardware device, providing low-level control. Example: The BIOS on a computer motherboard or the software on a printer.

A software-based emulation of a physical computer. A single physical machine can run multiple VMs, each with its own operating system and applications. Example: Running a Linux OS inside a window on your Windows PC using VMware.

A diverse group of techniques used in BI to discover knowledge. Includes Expert Systems (rules), Machine Learning (learns without explicit programming), Neural Networks (learns by example), and Genetic Algorithms (evolutionary approach). Example: Netflix's recommendation engine uses machine learning.

A relationship between two tables where a record in one table (the 'one') can be associated with multiple records in another table (the 'many'), but a record in the 'many' table can only be associated with one record in the 'one' table. Example: One advisor can have many students, but each student has only one primary advisor.

An AI technique that captures the tacit knowledge of a human expert as a set of rules in a software system. It consists of a knowledge base (the rules) and an inference engine (which applies the rules). Example: A system used by a bank to determine loan eligibility by applying a set of rules defined by experienced loan officers.

An AI technique where systems learn and improve from experience without being explicitly programmed. Algorithms are trained on large datasets to find patterns. Example: A spam filter that learns to identify new types of junk mail by analyzing emails you mark as spam.

A person, place, thing, or event about which data is stored in a database. In a database design, an entity becomes a table. Example: In a university database, 'Student', 'Professor', and 'Course' are all entities.

A characteristic or quality that describes an entity. In a database table, attributes become the columns (fields). Example: For the 'Student' entity, attributes would be 'Student_ID', 'FirstName', 'LastName', and 'Major'.

The process of defining, verifying, and controlling what is and is not included in a project. It ensures the project includes all the work required, and only the work required, to complete the project successfully. Example: Creating a detailed project charter that lists all deliverables, like 'user login page' and 'admin dashboard', and explicitly excludes others, like 'mobile app integration'.

A project is a temporary undertaking with a defined beginning and end to create a unique product or result. A program is a collection of interrelated projects managed together to obtain benefits not available from managing them individually. Example: Building a new website is a project. A company's entire 'Digital Transformation Initiative', which includes the website project, a CRM implementation project, and a data analytics project, is a program.

A technology that uses radio waves to read information stored on a tag attached to an object. An RFID system consists of a tag (with a microchip), a reader, and a host computer. Example: Automated toll collection systems (like EZ-Pass) where a reader on the toll booth communicates with an RFID tag on a car's windshield.

In Tableau, fields are classified as either discrete or continuous. Discrete fields (blue) have individually separate and distinct values, used for headers and labels. Continuous fields (green) have values that form an unbroken whole, used for axes. Example: 'Region' (North, South) is discrete (blue). 'Sales' ($100, $100.50, $101) is continuous (green).

The standard language used to create and structure the content of web pages. It uses 'tags' to define elements like headings, paragraphs, and links. Example: `

My Website

` is HTML code that creates a top-level heading with the text 'My Website'.

The set of rules for transferring files (text, images, sound, video) on the World Wide Web. It is the foundation of data communication for the web. Example: When you type a URL in your browser, it sends an HTTP request to the web server to retrieve the web page.

A relationship between two tables where one record in Table A can relate to many records in Table B, and one record in Table B can relate to many records in Table A. This requires a third 'junction' table to implement. Example: A 'Student' can enroll in many 'Courses', and a 'Course' can have many 'Students'. A 'Student_Course' junction table would link them.

traps.text: ★ Creating meaningful reports is NOT part of the ETL process. This is FALSE because ETL's purpose is to Extract, Transform, and Load data *into* a data warehouse. Reporting and analysis are subsequent steps performed by BI tools on the loaded data.

★ Assuming a project can absorb a scope change without affecting time or budget is WRONG. The Triple Constraint (Scope, Time, Resources) dictates that changing one variable forces a change in at least one of the others.
★ Confusing a Data Mart with a Data Warehouse is incorrect. A Data Mart is a *subset* of a Data Warehouse, tailored for a specific business line (e.g., Marketing), not the entire enterprise.

Using the Transform function in ETL for report-specific calculations is WRONG. This is incorrect because it compromises the integrity and neutrality of the data warehouse. Transformations should only be for cleansing and standardizing data for general use.

Treating a project as solely an IT project is WRONG. This is incorrect because almost all strategic projects are cross-functional and require business process changes, stakeholder buy-in, and management support to succeed.
Believing tasks not on the critical path can be delayed indefinitely is FALSE. While they have 'slack time', exceeding this slack will turn them into critical path tasks and delay the entire project.

Confusing data with information is incorrect. Data are raw, unorganized facts, while information is data that has been processed, organized, and structured to be meaningful. Raw sales figures are data; a report showing sales trends by region is information.
Assuming you own software you've paid for is FALSE. You own a *license* to use the software under specific terms, not the software itself.

Thinking a database with redundant data is acceptable is WRONG. Data redundancy leads to inconsistency (e.g., a customer's address updated in one place but not another) and other integrity problems. Normalization is used to prevent this.

Ignoring the user-designer communication gap is a common cause of project failure. It is WRONG to assume users and developers have the same understanding and priorities; this gap must be actively managed.

Confusing Wi-Fi and Bluetooth is incorrect. Bluetooth is for short-range Personal Area Networks (PANs) connecting a few devices (e.g., headset to phone), while Wi-Fi is for longer-range Local Area Networks (LANs) providing internet access.

Assuming a query on two tables without a JOIN or WHERE condition is correct is WRONG. This will produce a Cartesian product, matching every row from the first table with every row from the second, resulting in incorrect and massive result sets.

Using the ETL 'Transform' step to format data for a specific report is WRONG because the data warehouse should store standardized, cleansed data. Report-specific formatting must be done in the reporting application itself.
Accepting data redundancy (the same data stored in multiple places) in a database is WRONG because it leads to data inconsistency, where an update in one place is not reflected in the others.
Thinking the vendor manages everything in IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) is FALSE because with IaaS, you are still responsible for managing the OS, middleware, runtime, data, and applications.
Creating a Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) with excessive detail is WRONG because it becomes unmanageable. The rule is 'do not list more detail than you can manage.'

Assuming Bring Your Own Device (BYOD) only has advantages is FALSE because it introduces significant risks like data loss, loss of control over corporate data, and security vulnerabilities from malware.

Running a SELECT query on two tables without a WHERE clause or JOIN condition is WRONG because it produces a Cartesian product (every row from table A combined with every row from table B), which is usually meaningless and computationally expensive.

Using a Tableau JOIN when data sources are at different levels of granularity is incorrect because it can cause data duplication; a BLEND is required to aggregate data from each source *before* combining.
Assuming a Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) shows task dependencies is WRONG; it only outlines tasks and effort. A Gantt or PERT chart is required to show dependencies and timelines.

Believing normalization completely eliminates all data redundancy is incorrect; it minimizes *harmful* redundancy, but some repetition (like foreign keys) is necessary to maintain relationships between tables.

Assuming 'open source' software means it's completely free of rules is FALSE; it still has licenses (e.g., MIT, GPL) that govern its use, modification, and distribution, often requiring attribution or other obligations.
Thinking the ETL 'LOAD' step is just for data dumping is WRONG because it also involves crucial organizing, relating, and cataloging of data using metadata to make it useful for analysis.

Confusing a program with a project is incorrect. A program is a larger, strategic collection of multiple interrelated projects, while a project is a single, temporary endeavor with a specific outcome.
